summary: Describes a way to use GSS-API to give a secure channel between a client and server, authenticating the client with a password and the server with a public key certificate. It is on the standards track.

plainLanguage.summary: You use a password to prove who you are, while the server shows an ID card. Together they set up a private channel without needing a card of your own.

questions: how does lipkey send a password
subtitle: A thin GSS-API layer that lets a client log in with a password over a channel secured by the server's certificate, like a typical TLS setup.

tldr.problem: GSS-API mechanisms such as Kerberos V5 and SPKM need a lot of infrastructure, while the common TLS setup needs only a server certificate and a password database.
tldr.mechanism: LIPKEY sits on top of a variant of SPKM called SPKM-3. SPKM-3 authenticates the server and builds an encrypted channel, then LIPKEY sends the user name and password through it.
tldr.outcome: Applications already written for GSS-API get TLS-style low infrastructure security without changing their protocols. The RFC is a Proposed Standard and the unit metadata lists no replacement.

today: RFC 2847 is a Proposed Standard from June 2000, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: Why LIPKEY Exists
sections.content:
GSS-API gives an application protocol authentication, integrity and privacy. TLS does the same job, but GSS-API can fit better where the application runs over connectionless protocols, or where the protocol has its own security architecture, as ONC RPC does.

The catch is infrastructure. The better known GSS-API mechanisms, Kerberos V5 and SPKM, require a great deal of infrastructure to set up. A typical TLS deployment needs only a client with a list of trusted Certification Authorities and a server with a public key certificate and a password database. The RFC calls this the low infrastructure security model.

LIPKEY is a new GSS-API mechanism that reproduces that model by layering a thin mechanism over SPKM.
sections.plainLanguage: Some locks need a whole building of guards to work. LIPKEY is a simple lock: the shop shows its ID and you give a password.

sections.title: SPKM-3, the Mechanism Underneath
sections.content:
SPKM-1 with unilateral authentication is close to what is needed. The changes LIPKEY wants stretch RFC 2025 far enough that compatibility would be in danger, so the RFC defines a new mechanism type, SPKM-3. It is equivalent to SPKM-1 except for the changes listed in the RFC. LIPKEY requires an SPKM implementation that supports SPKM-3.

SPKM-3 has its own mechanism OID. It must also support all the mechanism-independent name types of RFC 2078.
sections.plainLanguage: SPKM-3 is a slightly changed copy of an older lock, with a new label so nobody mixes the two up.

sections.title: Required Algorithms
sections.content:
SPKM-3 MUST implement these algorithms, in addition to the REQUIRED ones from RFC 2025 (except md5WithRSAEncryption):

  • NULL-MAC (integrity): returns a zero length bit string. The initiator may have no certificate for itself or the target, so it cannot compute a real integrity value in its first token.
  • id-dsa-with-sha1 (integrity): the signature algorithm from RFC 2459.
  • HMAC-MD5 (integrity): a stronger MAC than the recommended 56 bit DES-MAC. An initiator without a certificate cannot use a digital signature once the context is established, so it needs a MAC.
  • cast5CBC (confidentiality): with the key length set to 128 bits. The RFC prefers it over triple DES, which is much slower, and over RC4, which has intellectual property concerns.
  • dhKeyAgreement (key establishment): required because RSAEncryption is of no use when the target cannot be mapped to a certificate.
  • id-sha1 (one-way function for subkey derivation): required because MD5 has been found to have weaknesses as a hash.

md5WithRSAEncryption and sha1WithRSAEncryption are only RECOMMENDED. md5WithRSAEncryption cannot be required because of intellectual property considerations, but is strongly recommended so LIPKEY can use existing public key infrastructure.
sections.plainLanguage: The RFC lists the exact locks and scramblers everyone must have, so both sides can always find one they both know.

sections.title: Context Tokens and Negotiation
sections.content:
RFC 2025 uses three tokens: REQ-TOKEN from the initiator, REP-TI-TOKEN from the target, and REP-IT-TOKEN back from the initiator. Because LIPKEY uses unilateral authentication, REP-IT-TOKEN is not used. The syntax of the SPKM-3 tokens is the same as SPKM-1.

The requirements on the first two tokens are:

  • If the initiator cannot compute req-integrity for lack of a target certificate, it MUST use NULL-MAC.
  • If the only key establishment algorithm offered is dhKeyAgreement, the target-certif-data-required bit MUST be set to 1.
  • If a weaker algorithm is supported, cast5CBC and HMAC-MD5 MUST be listed before it, to encourage the target to pick the stronger one.
  • The target MUST NOT use NULL-MAC. It MUST use a signature algorithm such as id-dsa-with-sha1, md5WithRSAEncryption or sha1WithRSAEncryption.
  • If the request used NULL-MAC, the target MUST compute rep-ti-integ over the concatenation of the req-contents and rep-ti-contents.

The RFC also adds new values to the algorithm fields of the quality of protection (QOP): confidentiality value 2 is cast5CBC, and integrity values 3, 4 and 5 are id-dsa-with-sha1, HMAC-MD5 and sha1WithRSAEncryption. Older SPKM-1 and SPKM-2 peers do not recognise these values and will not select them.
sections.plainLanguage: Both sides swap lists of the scramblers they know. Each lists its strongest first, so the other side picks a strong one.

sections.title: How the Initiator and Target Behave
sections.content:
The initiator's credentials are a user name and password. How they are obtained depends on the operating environment, for example a pop-up window. When LIPKEY first calls SPKM-3 for the initiator, it uses a NULL credential handle, mutual_req_flag FALSE, anon_req_flag TRUE and a NULL input token.

If the application asked for an anonymous context (anon_req_flag TRUE), LIPKEY simply returns the SPKM-3 outputs and gets out of the way, because LIPKEY tokens have no way to say the initiator is anonymous.

Otherwise the flow is: SPKM-3 context setup completes, then LIPKEY uses GSS_Wrap with conf_req_flag TRUE on the SPKM-3 context to encrypt the user name and password, and sends that as a second token. The target unwraps it and checks it against its user name and password database. It answers with a wrapped boolean, and the initiator maps TRUE to GSS_S_COMPLETE and FALSE to GSS_S_FAILURE. Because the user name and password must be sent over the secure channel, mutual_req_flag is ignored: unilateral authentication is impossible.

For other operations the LIPKEY context acts as a pass through to the SPKM-3 context.
sections.plainLanguage: First you check the shop's ID and open a private tube. Then you pass your password through the tube, and the shopkeeper answers yes or no.

sections.title: LIPKEY Tokens
sections.content:
LIPKEY has its own mechanism type OID. Until the SPKM-3 context is established, LIPKEY tokens are SPKM-3 tokens (an SPKMInnerContextToken as defined in RFC 2025), wrapped in a LIPKEY InitialContextToken for the first one.

After that there is one token each way. The initiator sends a GSS_Wrap of a UserName-Password value, a sequence of two OCTET STRINGs, each a UTF-8 string. The target replies with a GSS_Wrap of Valid-UNP, a BOOLEAN that is TRUE if the pair was valid. The target's wrap may or may not use confidentiality.

GSS_GetMIC and GSS_Wrap tokens are exactly what SPKM-3 produces, and LIPKEY does not interpret QOP values, so it supports the same QOPs as SPKM-3.
sections.plainLanguage: There are only two notes after the setup: your name and password in a sealed envelope, and a yes-or-no note back.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The password travels encrypted with 128 bit cast5CBC, so the main risk is how the target treats it afterwards. The target should clear memory and disk buffers holding the password, and any hash of it, immediately after validating it.

The initiator needs a list of trusted Certification Authorities to verify rep-ti-integ. If it meets a certificate signed by an unknown or untrusted authority it MUST NOT silently accept it, and must get confirmation from the user.

The RFC also argues that MD5's known weaknesses do not affect HMAC-MD5, and defends cast5CBC as a sound mandatory choice.
sections.plainLanguage: Once the shopkeeper has checked your password, they must shred it. And if the shop's ID looks fake, you must ask the user before trusting it.
